patterns.title: Batch medallion with Spark Declarative Pipelines
patterns.stackLine: Spark 4.3, Apache Iceberg and Unity Catalog with bronze, silver and gold
patterns.tagline: Declare the tables, let Spark work out the order, keep every layer in an open format.
patterns.definition: A batch medallion architecture organizes lakehouse tables into three layers: bronze holds raw records as they arrived, silver holds cleaned and conformed records, and gold holds aggregates shaped for a specific use. In this open reference architecture, Spark Declarative Pipelines (Spark 4.1 and later) defines each layer as a table or materialized view, Spark resolves the dependency graph and runs it, the tables are Apache Iceberg in Unity Catalog OSS 0.7 on S3-compatible storage, Apache Airflow schedules and backfills the runs, and DuckDB reads the gold tables through the catalog's Iceberg REST endpoint.
whenToUse: Your sources arrive as files, extracts or database snapshots on a schedule.
You want idempotent bronze loads and reproducible silver and gold tables.
You want to change a transformation without hand-ordering every downstream job.
notFor: Sub-second latency: use the real-time streaming pattern.
Teams that need a released Iceberg runtime for Spark 4.3 today: the course builds one from an open Iceberg pull request as a temporary step.

learn.label: AUTO CDC in Spark Declarative Pipelines

faqs.q: What is a medallion architecture?
faqs.a: A layout of lakehouse tables in three layers: bronze for raw data as it arrived, silver for cleaned and conformed data, and gold for aggregates built for a specific consumer.

faqs.q: Do I need Databricks to use declarative pipelines?
faqs.a: No. Spark Declarative Pipelines is part of open source Apache Spark from 4.1, run with the spark-pipelines CLI against a Spark Connect server.

faqs.q: Can DuckDB read tables that Spark writes?
faqs.a: Yes, when both go through the same catalog. In the masterclass, DuckDB attaches Unity Catalog's Iceberg REST endpoint and reads the gold Iceberg tables Spark wrote.

patterns.title: Change data capture with SCD type 2
patterns.stackLine: AUTO CDC in Spark Declarative Pipelines, from a Kafka change feed into Apache Iceberg
patterns.tagline: Keep the current state and every past version of each row, without hand-written MERGE logic.
patterns.definition: Change data capture (CDC) with slowly changing dimensions type 2 turns a feed of row-level changes from an operational system into a table that holds both the current state and the full history of each row. In open source Apache Spark 4.3, an AUTO CDC flow in Spark Declarative Pipelines reads the change feed, orders events by a sequence column, applies inserts, updates and deletes by key, and stores the result as SCD type 2: a change to a tracked column closes the old version and opens a new one, while changes to untracked columns update the current version in place. The target must support row-level operations, which Apache Iceberg provides.
whenToUse: An operational database or service emits change events and you need its tables in the lakehouse.
Auditors or analysts ask what a row looked like at a past point in time.
You want to stop maintaining hand-written MERGE statements for every replicated table.
notFor: Targets without row-level operations: AUTO CDC needs a DSv2 table that supports them.
Spark releases before 4.3 for this exact flow; the reference demo is verified on Spark 4.3.0.

steps.title: Apply by key, in order
steps.body: The AUTO CDC flow groups events by key and orders them by the sequence column, so late or out-of-order events land correctly.

steps.title: Track history
steps.body: A change to a tracked column (price or station in the demo) closes the current version and opens a new one; a change to another column updates the current version in place; a delete closes the row's window.

steps.title: Query any point in time
steps.body: The Iceberg table holds every version with its validity window, so you can read the current state or the state at any past sequence.

learn.label: AUTO CDC: turning an event log into current state

faqs.q: What is SCD type 2?
faqs.a: Slowly changing dimension type 2 keeps every version of a row: when a tracked attribute changes, the current version is closed and a new one is opened, so the table answers both what is true now and what was true at any earlier time.

faqs.q: Can open source Spark do CDC without hand-written MERGE?
faqs.a: Yes. Spark Declarative Pipelines in Spark 4.3 has AUTO CDC flows: you declare the keys, the sequence column, the delete condition and STORED AS SCD TYPE 1 or 2, and Spark applies the change feed.

faqs.q: How does AUTO CDC handle out-of-order events?
faqs.a: It orders events per key by the SEQUENCE BY column, so an event that arrives late is applied in sequence order rather than arrival order.

patterns.title: Streaming medallion
patterns.stackLine: Kafka, Spark Structured Streaming and Delta Lake in Unity Catalog
patterns.tagline: Events in, governed tables out, minutes or seconds behind the source.
patterns.definition: A streaming medallion architecture applies the bronze, silver and gold layout to event streams. Apache Kafka buffers events, an Apache Spark Structured Streaming job appends them to a bronze Delta Lake table with exactly-once checkpointing, and downstream streaming or declarative pipelines keep silver and gold tables up to date. Because the tables are open and registered in Unity Catalog OSS, batch jobs, BI tools and other engines read the same data the stream writes.
whenToUse: Sources emit events continuously and consumers want tables, not topics.
Latency of seconds to minutes is enough.
You want one copy of history that both streaming and batch jobs read.
notFor: Request-path latency in milliseconds: see the real-time streaming pattern.

Kafka is not registered in the catalog in the open-lakehouse stack; only the tables are.

faqs.q: How do I stream Kafka into Delta Lake with open source tools?
faqs.a: Run an Apache Spark Structured Streaming query with the Kafka source and a Delta sink with a checkpoint location; register the table in Unity Catalog OSS so other engines can find it.

faqs.q: Is the Kafka to Delta write exactly-once?
faqs.a: Yes for the table: Structured Streaming records Kafka offsets in its checkpoint and commits each micro-batch to the Delta log atomically, so a restarted query neither skips nor duplicates batches.

patterns.title: Real-time streaming with Spark Real-Time Mode
patterns.stackLine: Kafka in, Kafka out, milliseconds in between
patterns.tagline: Continuous processing for fraud, recommendations and live boards, measured end to end.
patterns.definition: Real-time streaming is the architecture for decisions that must happen while an event is still in flight: score a payment, update a recommendation, move a leaderboard. In open source Apache Spark, Real-Time Mode is a Structured Streaming trigger that processes records continuously instead of in micro-batches. The reference pipelines read from Kafka, transform or keep state with transformWithState, and write back to Kafka or a key-value store, with latency measured from producer timestamp to consumer.
whenToUse: Your SLA is in tens or hundreds of milliseconds, not seconds.
You are porting Apache Flink jobs and want to know which ones move to Spark.
You already run Spark for batch and want one engine for both.
notFor: Writing large analytical tables: use the streaming medallion pattern and keep this path thin.
Python UDFs in the hot path: Real-Time Mode does not support them.

caveats: Open source Spark 4.1 Real-Time Mode is stateless only; stateful queries need a later release (the stateful demos run on Spark 4.3).

faqs.q: How fast is Spark Real-Time Mode?
faqs.a: In the spark-rtm-quickstart run committed in results/latency-results.md (stateless, 500 events per second, 16 cores), end-to-end p50 was 17 ms and p99 was 21 to 26 ms across six runs. In spark-demos demo 14 on Spark 4.3.0, a stateless enrichment step measured p50 0 ms and p99 1 ms in real-time mode against 115 ms and 204 ms in micro-batch.

faqs.q: Can Spark replace Flink for low-latency streaming?
faqs.a: For many stateless and windowed jobs, yes; flink-to-spark-rtm writes the same four patterns for both engines. Keyed state with timers is where migrations need the most care, since Spark expresses it through transformWithState.

faqs.q: Does Real-Time Mode support stateful queries?
faqs.a: Not in open source Spark 4.1. The stateful reference demos (transformWithState, dedup and windows) run on Spark 4.3.

patterns.title: One catalog, many engines
patterns.stackLine: Unity Catalog OSS with Spark, DuckDB, PyIceberg and Trino on Delta and Iceberg
patterns.tagline: Write once, read from whatever engine fits the question.
patterns.definition: A multi-engine catalog architecture puts an open catalog between the tables and every engine that uses them. Unity Catalog OSS stores table metadata in Postgres, exposes Delta tables through its own API and Iceberg tables through the Iceberg REST catalog specification, and vends short-lived storage credentials per table. Apache Spark, DuckDB, PyIceberg and Trino then read and write the same data without copies, and access is decided once, in the catalog.
whenToUse: Different teams prefer different engines for the same data.
You want to stop copying data into a warehouse per tool.
You want storage credentials vended per table instead of shared keys.
notFor: Expecting identical feature support in every engine: write support differs by engine, format and catalog version.

faqs.q: What is an Iceberg REST catalog?
faqs.a: An HTTP API defined by the Apache Iceberg project for creating, loading and committing Iceberg tables. Any engine that speaks it can use any catalog that implements it, including Unity Catalog OSS, Apache Polaris and Lakekeeper.

faqs.q: Can Spark and DuckDB share the same tables?
faqs.a: Yes. Point both at the same catalog: Spark through the Unity Catalog connector or Iceberg REST, DuckDB through its Iceberg extension attached to the Iceberg REST endpoint.

faqs.q: What is credential vending?
faqs.a: The catalog hands an engine short-lived storage credentials scoped to one table's location when the engine loads it, so engines never hold long-lived bucket keys.

patterns.title: Governed AI agents for data engineering
patterns.stackLine: Spark Declarative Pipelines, Spark Connect, Kubernetes and a governed Iceberg REST catalog
patterns.tagline: Agents write pipeline specs; the platform decides what they are allowed to touch.
patterns.definition: Governed AI data engineering is an architecture in which AI agents author data pipelines but never hold direct power over data. The agent writes declarative Spark Declarative Pipelines specs as a pull request; CI dry-runs them against the real catalog; a controller applies approved changes. Each tenant reaches Spark only through one identity-pinned Spark Connect ingress behind mTLS, executors run as Kubernetes pods, and a governed Iceberg REST catalog authorizes every request and vends storage credentials scoped to that tenant. Each layer owns one job, so a mistake in one does not become a breach in another.
whenToUse: You want AI agents to build or change pipelines without giving them production credentials.
You need per-tenant isolation on shared Spark infrastructure.

faqs.q: How do you let AI agents build data pipelines safely?
faqs.a: Give them a declarative output and no direct path to data: the agent writes Spark Declarative Pipelines specs as a pull request, CI dry-runs them against the real catalog, and execution happens through an identity-pinned Spark Connect ingress with a catalog that authorizes every table operation.

faqs.q: Do declarative pipelines catch more agent mistakes?

patterns.title: Open data sharing
patterns.stackLine: Delta Sharing servers over Unity Catalog and open tables
patterns.tagline: Share live tables with another organization without copying them or sending files.
patterns.definition: Open data sharing is an architecture for giving another organization read access to live lakehouse tables through an open protocol instead of file exports. A Delta Sharing server authenticates the recipient, checks which shares and tables they may read, and returns short-lived URLs or credentials for the underlying files; the recipient reads them with any Delta Sharing client, including pandas, Spark and other engines. Data stays in the provider's storage and the recipient always sees the current version.
whenToUse: Partners, customers or regulators need recurring access to the same tables.
You want to stop running file-drop jobs.
Recipients use different tools than you do.
notFor: Write access for recipients: the protocol is read-only.

patterns.title: Policy pushdown and open lineage
patterns.stackLine: Cedar policies compiled to CEL, enforced in Spark and DataFusion, with OpenLineage
patterns.tagline: Write access rules once, enforce them inside every engine, and record where every column came from.
patterns.definition: Policy pushdown and open lineage is a governance architecture for multi-engine lakehouses. Access rules are authored once in the Cedar policy language, compiled to portable CEL expressions, and enforced inside each query engine's plan as row filters and column masks, so no engine depends on SQL views or per-engine rewrites. Alongside, every job emits OpenLineage events, which are stored as lakehouse tables and served through a lineage API, so auditors can trace a published number back to its sources.
whenToUse: Several engines read the same sensitive tables.
You need row filters and column masks that cannot be bypassed by choosing a different engine.
Regulators or auditors ask where a value came from.
notFor: Production lineage storage today without evaluation: headwaters describes itself as experimental and recommends Marquez for production.

patterns.title: Semantic layer with Spark metric views
patterns.stackLine: Metrics declared in YAML, served over Spark Connect to BI, notebooks and agents
patterns.tagline: Define revenue once. Every dashboard, notebook and agent gets the same number.
patterns.definition: A semantic layer is the set of governed metric and dimension definitions that sit between tables and the tools that query them. In open source Apache Spark, a metric view declares measures and dimensions in YAML over a source table; consumers query it with the MEASURE() function and Spark expands the definition at query time. Served over Spark Connect or JDBC, the same definitions answer dashboards, notebooks and AI agents, so a metric cannot drift between tools.
whenToUse: Different teams report different numbers for the same metric.
You want AI agents to answer questions from governed definitions instead of writing raw SQL.
notFor: Spark versions before metric views shipped; the reference demo is verified on Spark 4.2.0.

patterns.definition: The ML lifecycle on an open lakehouse ties experiments, models and GenAI traces to versioned tables. Features are built by Spark from silver and gold tables in an open format; each MLflow run records parameters, metrics, artifacts and the table snapshot or version it trained on; the MLflow model registry promotes versions; and the MLflow AI Gateway fronts model providers for GenAI applications. You run GenAI applications and want tracing and evaluation in the same place.
notFor: Low-latency online feature serving by itself: pair it with the real-time streaming pattern and a key-value store.

patterns.title: Arrow-native serving
patterns.stackLine: Arrow Flight SQL and Spark Connect clients over lakehouse tables
patterns.tagline: Results leave as Arrow columns, not rows, in whatever language the client speaks.
patterns.definition: Arrow-native serving delivers lakehouse query results as Apache Arrow record batches over gRPC instead of row-by-row JDBC. Two open protocols do this: Arrow Flight SQL, a generic SQL-over-Flight protocol, and Spark Connect, Spark's client-server protocol. A Flight SQL server built on Apache DataFusion can answer queries over Delta tables with policy enforcement and lineage built in, while Spark Connect lets thin clients in Python, Go, Rust, Swift and other languages send plans to a remote Spark and hand the Arrow results straight to DuckDB or Polars.
whenToUse: Clients pull large result sets into Python, Rust or other analytical tools.
You want to query the lakehouse from a language without a JVM.
You want policy and lineage enforced at the serving edge.
notFor: Clients that only speak ODBC or JDBC: put a Flight SQL JDBC driver or a SQL gateway in front.
